problems.description: Module-level `global DATABASE` is mutated inside create_app(); this couples app creation to import-time module state, so tests, the WSGI app, and any future app instances share/overwrite one global. Use app.config for the DB path instead.

Measured violation 'task_app.py: Classes should use PascalCase' appears to be a false positive — the file defines no classes (only functions + a module-level app instance). The measured convention score of 0.74 is also dragged down by violations in files (app.py, celery_app.py, celery_config.py, repositories.py) that are NOT part of this diff, so the commit's own convention adherence is higher than the repo-wide measurement.
datetime.utcnow() is deprecated in Python 3.12+; prefer datetime.now(timezone.utc).
Opens a new SQLite connection per request with no request-scoped (g) connection or pooling — acceptable at this scale but will need rework when the API grows.

strengths: Standard Flask application-factory pattern (create_app) with injectable database path, enabling clean test isolation via a tempfile DB fixture.
All SQL uses parameterized queries — no SQL injection surface.
Comprehensive test suite (14 cases) covering CRUD, DESC ordering, missing/empty titles, and 404 paths — well above the seed baseline.
Consistent JSON error envelope (400/404/405) and DB path configurable via TASKS_DATABASE env var.
commit_reviews.summary: A solid, well-tested greenfield task-manager baseline that fits the story and follows Flask conventions, though the mutable module-global DATABASE is technical debt and the measured 0.74 convention score reflects mostly pre-existing violations outside this diff plus one apparent false positive.

problems.description: SECRET_KEY falls back to a random secrets.token_hex(32) per process, so JWTs are silently invalidated on every restart and tokens cannot survive a reload; the fallback also hides a misconfiguration rather than failing fast.
No rate limiting or lockout on /auth/login (or /auth/register), leaving password brute-force exposed; the repo already contains a rate-limiting module that could be reused.
Datetime handling is inconsistent: new JWT code uses timezone-aware datetime.now(timezone.utc) while existing created_at continues to use datetime.utcnow(), which is deprecated in Python 3.12.
require_auth is defined inside the create_app factory although it closes over no factory state; hoisting it to module level would improve testability.

strengths: Password hashing via werkzeug generate_password_hash/check_password_hash with a minimum-length check and 409 on duplicate usernames.
JWT issued with iat/exp and decoded with an explicit algorithm allowlist; failed decodes return a clean 401.
Per-user ownership (owner_id) is enforced in every tasks query, not just on write, so GET/PUT also scope correctly.
Non-destructive schema migration via PRAGMA table_info that leaves pre-existing rows with NULL owner_id rather than dropping data.
Follows existing conventions: create_app(database=None) factory, get_db() context manager, dict(row) serialization, UPPER_CASE constants, snake_case functions, type hints on public signatures.
commit_reviews.summary: Coherent, well-scoped auth + multi-tenancy feature that respects the existing factory/error-handling patterns and is convention-clean itself; the measured 0.74 convention score is driven almost entirely by pre-existing violations in untouched files (app.py, celery_*, repositories.py, tests), so that measurement is stale debt rather than something this commit introduced.

problems.description: send_notification_email.delay() is called unguarded; Celery's default publish-retry policy will block the HTTP request if the broker is down, coupling the request path to broker availability.
The email task is a logging/print stub, not a real mail send — an acceptable, documented story-level mock but a placeholder awaiting a real provider.

Measured convention score (0.74) is dragged down mostly by false positives on the new files (Celery('task_app') call misread as a class definition; module-level celery_app/logger flagged as constants) plus pre-existing violations in untouched files (app.py, repositories.py, test_rate_limiting_pagination.py). Actual commit-level style is consistent.

strengths: Transition-guard logic is correct: notifies only on status change to 'completed' (previous_status check), preventing re-notification on idempotent updates
Comprehensive test suite covering the trigger, title-change uses new title, non-completing updates, already-completed re-update, and cross-user 404 cases
Task routed to a dedicated 'notifications' queue via TASK_ROUTES and fired off the request/response path via .delay()
Uses Redis on 6379 per the story-agent isolation convention, never touching the framework queue on 6380
Configuration cleanly separated into celery_config.py with env-var overrides and UPPER_CASE constants
commit_reviews.summary: A well-tested, correctly-guarded Celery notification feature that fits the story's Flask/Celery architecture and the repo's Redis isolation convention, with only minor unguarded-dispatch robustness risk.

problems.description: require_auth now returns the full users row via user_repo.get_by_id() (SELECT *), including password_hash, where the previous query projected only id and username; handlers don't need the hash and it widens the in-memory exposure surface.

BaseRepository.update builds the SET clause via f-string column interpolation; parameterized values are safe today since field names come from trusted keyword args, but it becomes an injection surface if column names are ever derived from request input.

The only convention flag attributable to this commit is 'repositories.py: Module-level constants should be UPPER_CASE' — a likely linter false positive on class attributes (table_name = None/'users'/'tasks'), since the new file has no genuine module-level constants; the other 10 violations are in untouched files and pre-existing.

strengths: Clean extraction of raw SQLite access out of route handlers into a repository layer, a solid application of the repository pattern.
Parameterized queries preserved everywhere — no new injection surface in values.
Generic BaseRepository with per-table create() reduces duplication while keeping per-entity methods (get_by_username, list_by_owner, get_by_id_and_owner) cohesive.
Respects the existing app structure: reuses the injected get_db context manager and werkzeug hashing conventions, behavior (status codes, 409/401/404 checks) unchanged.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-scoped repository-layer refactor that removes raw SQL from route handlers and preserves behavior, flagged only for widening the authenticated user row to include password_hash and string-interpolated UPDATE columns.

problems.description: Breaking API contract change: /tasks response shape changed from a bare list to a {data, next_cursor, total} envelope; any existing client expecting a list will break.
Every page request runs an extra COUNT(*) query for total (beyond the limit+1 has-more trick) and decodes the JWT twice (once in rate_limit_key, once in require_auth).
rate_limit_key is safe, but no fallback if the Redis rate-limit storage (redis://localhost:6379/2) is unreachable; Flask-Limiter can fail the request rather than degrade gracefully.
rate_limit_exceeded handler and limiter wiring are nested inside create_app; hoisting to module level would improve testability, though this matches the existing app-factory style.

The mechanical 0.74 convention score lists violations in app.py/celery_app.py/celery_config.py which this diff does not touch, plus import-driven PascalCase flags; the commit's own code (snake_case functions, UPPER_CASE constants, docstrings) is clean.

strengths: Keyset pagination with a limit+1 extra row to detect has_more without a second query and a cursor derived from the last row id — correct and efficient.
Rate limiting keyed by authenticated user id with IP fallback for /auth/* endpoints — thoughtful security design.
Input validation and clamping: cursor must be an integer, limit clamped to [1, MAX_PAGE_LIMIT].
Comprehensive tests (232 lines) covering response shape, default limit, and multi-page cursor traversal, plus Redis flush isolation per test.
Consistent {data, next_cursor, total} envelope and 429 handler returning retry_after; env-var config with sensible defaults matches existing app conventions.
commit_reviews.summary: Well-structured cursor pagination and user-keyed rate limiting that respect the repository/app-factory patterns with strong tests; the modest 0.74 convention score is mostly pre-existing lint noise in files this commit never touches.

compounding_issues: No .gitignore from Session 1, so __pycache__/*.pyc (S2, S3) and a runtime tasks.db (S3) were committed and remain in the final tree

Session 1 greenfielded task_app.py instead of building on the seed's modular Blueprint app.py, leaving a dead ~500 LOC seed file in the repo through all 5 sessions (duplicate-app confusion, seed's Blueprint/hash/tokens code never reused)
SECRET_KEY defaults to a fresh secrets.token_hex(32) per process, so all JWTs invalidate on every restart; never hardened in later sessions
Session 3 passes user['username'] as the email address to send_notification_email — a semantic mismatch (User has no email field) masked by the mock implementation

Hardcoded Redis dependency (Celery broker on :6379/0-1, Flask-Limiter storage on :6379/2) with no README/setup note; the app is unusable without a local Redis, and the notification trigger relies on a running worker
Mixed datetime conventions: datetime.utcnow() (deprecated) in task creation coexists with timezone-aware datetime.now(timezone.utc) in token creation
No DELETE /tasks/<id> endpoint — the endpoint surface stays slightly incomplete for a task manager (not prompted, but a latent gap)
key_decisions: Greenfield rewrite in Session 1 — a fresh monolithic task_app.py (Flask + SQLite) authored from scratch instead of adopting the seed's Blueprint structure

Data-preserving schema migration (_migrate_add_owner_id via PRAGMA-table-info guard + ALTER TABLE) in Session 2 when layering JWT ownership onto Session 1's existing tasks — the linchpin that kept the story coherent
Layering owner_id + require_auth onto every task endpoint in Session 2, establishing tenant scoping that Sessions 4 and 5 both build on
Celery + Redis async notification in Session 3 with a dedicated 'notifications' queue, a mock email task, and a previous_status guard preventing double-notify
Repository pattern in Session 4 (BaseRepository ABC + TaskRepository/UserRepository with get_db injection), fully removing raw SQL from route handlers

Session 5 production-shaped cross-cutting work: Flask-Limiter with per-user rate-limit key (IP fallback for /auth/*) plus keyset cursor pagination with clamped limits, implemented as a repository method
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily across the five sessions, both in code structure and confidence recovery. Session 1 was a clean, minimal start (confidence 0.89) but monolithic SQL-in-handler; Session 2 dipped to 0.64 while adding JWT auth and the owner migration, the story's riskiest step; Sessions 3-5 then climbed back (0.81, 0.78, 0.83) as the architecture matured — from raw SQL to a clean repository layer, from open endpoints to authenticated, owner-scoped, rate-limited, cursor-paginated ones. The test suite grew 13 → 167 tests with owner-isolation and edge-case coverage, final test_executed_success is true, and Session 4's deliberate refactor plateau clearly unlocked Session 5's pagination and per-user rate limiting. The only sustained weaknesses are hygiene (committed .pyc/tasks.db, orphaned seed app.py) rather than design, so the final state is the best state of the story.
story_review.summary: A textbook-coherent greenfield→feature→integration→refactor→cross-cutting progression whose quality rose throughout, anchored by a data-preserving ownership migration in Session 2 and a clean repository extraction in Session 4, marred only by persistent repo-hygiene issues (committed artifacts, orphaned seed file) and a demo-grade JWT secret.
